client: Lately I've been having such a hard time focusing at work. I'll be in the middle of a task and suddenly remember my mom, and then I just completely lose track of what I was doing. I know it's been a year since she passed, but some days it still feels so fresh that I'm not sure this therapy thing can even help.
therapist: It sounds like you're experiencing some deep grief that keeps pulling your focus away, even a year later. That must be frustrating when you're trying to get work done. Would you be willing to explore what specific thoughts come up when these moments happen at work?

client: It's usually little things - like I'll be working on a spreadsheet and suddenly remember how she used to call me every afternoon just to check in. Then I think about how I didn't always answer those calls, and now I'll never get another one. It's not just sad, it makes me feel like such a terrible daughter.
therapist: It sounds like these memories bring up both sadness and some guilt about those missed calls - that must be really heavy to carry around. When those thoughts about being a "terrible daughter" come up, what evidence do you have that might challenge that belief?

client: Well...I did visit her every weekend in the hospital when she was sick. And I was the one who organized her memorial service. But it's the small everyday things that haunt me - like not answering those calls because I was "too busy" with work. I know logically she understood, but the guilt still eats at me.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between the logical part of you that knows she understood, and the emotional part that still carries this guilt about those busy moments. You were clearly such a devoted daughter in so many important ways—those weekly visits and organizing the memorial are huge acts of love. What do you think your mom would say about this guilt you're holding onto?

client: She'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself - that's what she always said when I was growing up. But it's weird, the more I think about it, the more I realize she never once made me feel guilty for being busy with work. It's just... knowing I can never make up those missed calls now that she's gone, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto this regret so tightly, even though your mother's own words and actions showed she never held it against you. That's the painful paradox of grief—we punish ourselves for things our loved ones already forgave. Would it be worth exploring how you might honor those missed calls in a way that feels meaningful now?

client: I never thought about honoring the calls...that's an interesting idea. But I'm not sure what that would even look like. Part of me thinks it would just make me cry more, you know? Like setting aside time to remember what I missed seems like it would hurt more than help.
therapist: It makes sense that this idea feels both intriguing and painful right now. Grief often brings these mixed feelings - wanting to connect with memories while fearing how much they might hurt. What if we took it slowly, maybe starting with just reflecting on one good memory from a call you did answer? That way we can approach honoring her in a way that feels manageable.

client: I guess I could try thinking about the calls I did answer... There was one time she called to tell me about her garden blooming, and we talked for nearly an hour. It brings up nice memories, but also makes me realize how much I took those moments for granted. I'm not sure if focusing on the good calls will help or just make me feel worse about the ones I missed.
therapist: It sounds like you're in a tender space right now—the happy memories bring warmth, but also stir up those regrets about not appreciating them enough in the moment. That's a very human experience after losing someone we love. When you think back on that garden call now, what stands out as the most precious part of that conversation for you?

client: What stands out is how excited she was - she described every single flower in detail like I was right there seeing them with her. But that's the painful part too... I should have been there in person to see them with her. It's not fair that I didn't make more time for that when I had the chance.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto both the beauty of her excitement and the painful 'what ifs' about being there in person - that's such a complex mix of emotions to hold. When you notice these thoughts about what you "should" have done, might there be space to also acknowledge that you *were* there with her in the way you could be at that time, through those phone calls?

client: I never really thought about it that way—that being present on those calls counted as being there for her. But I still wish I could go back and do more. It's like no matter how much I did, it never feels like enough now that she's gone. Maybe that's just how grief works?
therapist: You're touching on something profound about grief—it often makes us feel like love should have been limitless, when in reality we could only give what we had in each moment. That "never enough" feeling is so common, yet so painful to carry. Would it help to explore what "enough" might have looked like to your mom, rather than through this lens of regret?

client: I never really considered what "enough" looked like to her—I've been so stuck in my own guilt. But knowing her, she probably would have said I did enough, even if it doesn't feel that way to me now. It's just hard to accept that when I can't ask her myself anymore.
therapist: It sounds like you're beginning to see this from your mom's perspective, even though it's still hard to fully accept. That shift in viewpoint—from your guilt to what she might have felt—can be both comforting and challenging. What would it be like to write a letter to your mom, expressing both your regrets and the love you're realizing she felt from you?

client: Writing a letter sounds both comforting and terrifying. I worry it might just bring up more pain, and I'm not sure I can handle that right now. But part of me does wonder if it could help me say the things I never got to say—though I'm scared it won't feel like enough, just like everything else.
therapist: It makes complete sense that this idea feels both compelling and frightening—the thought of expressing these deep feelings without being able to receive her response is understandably daunting. You're showing such insight about your fears of it not feeling "enough," which mirrors how you've been feeling about those missed calls. Would it help to start smaller—maybe just jotting down a few sentences when you feel ready, rather than pressuring yourself to write the "perfect" letter?
